title: When practice fails you
hook: practice isn't a cure-all; get help when you need it
tomorrow: why would a text praise the one who fell?

segments.voice: Yesterday, life events and one line for them, bend, don't break: the Buddha's worn-out cart, still rolling with straps. Mai shrank her sit to fit the bakery shifts. This week, even the small sit stopped helping.
screen: `BEND, DON'T BREAK.` → `EVEN THE SMALL SIT STOPPED HELPING.`

segments.voice: Some nights the breathing that used to settle everything just doesn't. Mai's text came in the middle of the night: finals, early shifts, barely any sleep for days, and when she sits, her heart races louder instead of quieter. Practice was supposed to fix this. An old story looks at that moment from the other side. In the Vinaya, the Buddha is walking through the monks' lodgings with Ananda when they find a monk lying sick in his own mess, too weak to get up. Nobody has come to help him.
screen: `THE BREATHING STOPS WORKING.` → `A SICK MONK, ALONE.` → `NOBODY HAS COME.`

segments.voice: The Buddha asks him why no one tends him. Because I'm no use to the other monks, he says. So the Buddha and Ananda fetch water, wash him, and lift him onto a bed. Then the Buddha calls the monks together. You have no mother and no father here to look after you, he tells them. If you don't tend one another, who will? Whoever would tend me should tend the sick. That's the teaching: in Buddhism, caring for the sick isn't a break from the path; the Buddha puts it at the center. And getting care isn't failing at practice. The Vinaya has a whole section on the medicines monks may take. It even tells of Jivaka, a physician, treating the Buddha himself, with medicine given through lotus flowers to smell. Meditation was never meant to replace a doctor, a counselor, or a parent who notices. Mai told her mom, Linh, a pharmacist, and they made an appointment. It won't all be fixed by next week, and that's all right. If you're ever in danger, or thinking about hurting yourself, call or text 988 in the US, or your local emergency number. That's practice too.
screen: `THE BUDDHA WASHES THE SICK MONK.` · `IF YOU DON'T TEND ONE ANOTHER, WHO WILL?` · `MEDICINE IN THE VINAYA.` · `IN DANGER? 988 OR LOCAL HELP.` · then, large: `GET HELP TOO.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person you could actually tell if things got hard: a parent, a friend, a doctor, a teacher. Picture their face and the one sentence you'd say. If someone comes to mind who might need that from you, hold them too. Nothing to send; just know the door is there.
When practice fails you: the times meditation can't carry it alone. The Buddha took medicine, and told his monks to tend the sick.
Get help too: whoever would tend the Buddha, he said, should tend the sick. Take good care.

screen: `DAY 1758 COUNTS.` → `A LIFE OF PRACTICE · 33 OF 45.` → `TOMORROW: WHY WOULD A TEXT PRAISE THE ONE WHO FELL?`

howItsDone: Buddhist monasteries care for sick monks as the Vinaya directs, and monks may take medicine; teachers commonly encourage students to see a doctor or counselor alongside their practice when they're struggling.

fork.setup: your friend has felt panicky for weeks and hopes more meditation will fix it on its own. what fits today's story?
options: more meditation; if it isn't working, she's doing it wrong.
keep practicing, and also talk to a doctor or someone she trusts.

original.note: Pali: sick, ill. Tending the sick is what the Buddha asked of his monks: whoever would tend me should tend the sick.

trapdoor: what you thought: a serious practitioner doesn't need outside help.
what it means: the Buddha washed a sick monk himself and told his monks to tend the sick as they'd tend him.
what a scholar hears: Vinaya, Mahavagga VIII.26 for the sick monk, the chapter on medicines (Mahavagga VI), and Jivaka's treatment of the Buddha in Mahavagga VIII.1.
guess: times when practice alone can't carry what you face
a sign that you've chosen the wrong teacher
giving up meditation for good after a setback

chat.meaning: The Buddha washed a sick monk himself, told his monks to tend the sick, and was treated by the physician Jivaka. Getting care isn't failing at practice.

tie.story: The Buddha and Ananda washed a sick monk no one would tend, and the Buddha said whoever would tend him should tend the sick.
tie.friend: Mai told her mom and booked a doctor; that's part of practice, not a failure of it.
tie.you: who would you tell if things got hard?

Vinaya.meaning: the book of discipline for Buddhist monks and nuns

Jivaka.meaning: a physician who, the Vinaya says, treated the Buddha

sources.ref: Vinaya Pitaka, Mahavagga VIII.26 (the monk sick with dysentery; 'whoever would tend me should tend the sick')
Vinaya Pitaka, Mahavagga VIII.1 (Jivaka treats the Buddha with medicated lotuses)

notes: Shape: story. Mai's storyline: finals plus early bakery shifts, days of poor sleep, sitting makes her racing heart louder; she tells her mom Linh (a pharmacist) and books a doctor. Paced on purpose: not fixed by next week.

Crisis care: the teach includes 988 (US) or local emergency number for danger or self-harm, per the project's safety rule, and the screen repeats it. For parents: the hook mentions a monk lying sick 'in his own mess' (the text: dysentery, lying in his own urine and excrement), kept gentle.

Mahavagga VIII.26 paraphrased: the monk says the others don't tend him because he is of no use to them; the Buddha and Ananda wash him and lay him on a bed; 'you have no mother and no father who might tend you; if you do not tend one another, who will?'; 'whoever would tend me should tend the sick'. Confirm.
Jivaka (Mahavagga VIII.1): the Buddha's body is disordered; Jivaka treats him with lotuses infused with medicine to smell (a purgative). Count of lotus handfuls left out on purpose. Confirm.
Surprising fact: the Buddha himself took medicine from a physician, given through lotus flowers to smell (Vinaya).
